rationale: The first call copies at most n/2 elements, the next n/4, and so on, so time is O(n). Python has no tail-call elimination, so every slice stays alive as an argument to its callee, and the live slices sum to O(n). This assumes list input. Slicing a range, as some doctests do, is O(1), but the stated assumption covers that.

The bottom-up build is O(n), and the n−1 extractions each call heapify, which descends at most O(log n). Total is O(n log n). heapify recurses once per level with no TCO, so the stack is O(log n) and nothing else is allocated.

Each call halves the inclusive range with O(1) work, so time is O(log n). Java does not eliminate tail calls, so the stack reaches O(log n) frames. Analyzing find plus binsear and skipping main is the right scope.

T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) + O(1) gives Θ(φ^n), which is bounded above by O(2^n). The call chain along n−1 is n deep, so space is O(n). Θ(φ^n) is not Θ(2^n), so O(2^n) is a valid but loose upper bound; the packet accepts it as the coarse class.

Time is right. The split candidates sum to roughly d^3/6, which is Θ(d^3), and d versus M = d−1 does not change the class. The function returns a tuple containing both d×d tables (matrix and sol); under the project convention excluding returned output, those tables are excluded from auxiliary space. Only loop scalars remain, so revised auxiliary space is O(1).
expected_auxiliary_space_exact: O(1) auxiliary space excluding returned tables; output storage O(d^2)
assumptions: Analyze matrix_chain_order only. Let d = len(array) >= 2 and M = d - 1 matrices. Treat integer arithmetic and comparisons as O(1). Exclude the input list and both returned d-by-d tables (matrix and sol) from auxiliary space; include temporary storage and scalar loop state. Total returned output storage is O(d^2), while auxiliary space is O(1).
